subject: babaYagaHut
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: Baba Yaga's hut on chicken legs.
Style: Slavic folk art.

spec.name: Baba Yaga's Hut on Chicken Legs
spec.description: A folk-art log hut with a carved, painted roof, perched on two huge scaly chicken legs, with a skull-topped fence, a ladder and a glowing window.
spec.layout: A tall log cabin rests on two big yellow chicken legs standing apart on the ground (left leg +X, right leg -X). The hut's door and a short porch face +Z with a ladder-stair running down toward the front. The steep roof ridge runs along z, with carved end-boards (a sun and rooster motif) at front and back, and a stubby chimney. A fence of poles with glowing skulls arcs around the back and sides on the ground. Slavic folk art: bold flat colours, red, ochre and teal painted ornaments, zigzag and sun motifs on every board, rounded log ends, simple chunky shapes. Parts: legs and ground-claws, hut body logs, roof, porch with ladder, fence with skulls.

parts.builds: Two huge chicken legs: thick yellow tapering thigh, knee bend, shin and ankle with scale-ring bands in legDark, three forward toes and one rear toe each with claw spikes in claw colour, toe joint knuckle balls. Scaly feather tufts at the thigh in carveRed and cream. Chains named hipL/kneeL/ankleL and hipR/kneeR/ankleR, role leg, feet planted on y=0 toes spread in +Z.
parts.attaches: Thigh tops end at legHipL and legHipR under the hut floor.

parts.builds: Square log cabin walls 2.2 wide by 2.0 long and 1.5 tall: stacked horizontal log cylinders in log/logDark with logEnd round ends poking out at corners, a floor slab, a door in the front with carveRed frame, zigzag trim, iron hinges, a glowing window (window colour) with carved teal shutters on each side wall and a round one at the back, a painted sun disc beside the door.
parts.attaches: Sits on hutFloor on the legs; roof starts at eaveLine; porch attaches at doorFront.

parts.builds: Steep gabled roof in roof/roofDark with overhanging eaves, rows of rounded shingles as small boards, a carved ridge beam ending in rooster-head or horse-head finials in carveYellow and carveRed, gable end boards (pozarnye) at front and back with sun, zigzag and teardrop cut-outs in carveRed/carveYellow/carveTeal/cream, a stubby brick-and-log chimney with a little smoke puff in cream.
parts.attaches: Eaves rest on eaveLine over the cabin walls; ridge at mount ridge.

parts.builds: Small front porch deck in wood with two carved posts and a little pitched canopy in roofDark, painted carveRed balusters, and a steep ladder with rungs descending forward to y=0.4 where it ends in the air above a flat stone, with a cream-painted step. Hanging dried herb bundles and a tiny lantern in window glow colour.
parts.attaches: Deck at porchDeck meets the front wall at doorFront.

parts.builds: A ring-arc of sharpened pole fence in log/logDark around the sides and back, 0.7 to 1.4 tall poles of varied height, every third pole topped with a bone-coloured skull (sphere cranium, jaw box, dark eye sockets glowing skullGlow), a few rope bands in cream, a low grass-green ground pad disc in ground colour with a few tufts and mushrooms in carveRed with cream dots.
parts.attaches: Circles groundPad on the floor around the leg feet, clear of the legs and porch ladder.

calls.reasoning:
I'm working out how to build the fence function, considering whether static parts without a bone should attach to the nearest joint or just ride along with the hut's joint as scenery.

Now I'm sketching the geometry: a sunken ground pad disc, a box footprint for the legs, and a fence arc hugging the back and sides while leaving the front open, positioning the support poles near the leg bases.

Now I'm placing the fence poles around the arc, spacing roughly 17 posts over 220 degrees with sharpened cone tips and randomized heights between 0.7 and 1.4. Now I'm building the skull detail: a scaled cranium sphere, jaw box, dark eye sockets each with a small glowing green orb inside using the glow kit, oriented to face outward from the hut.

Still placing skull components...

I'll skip extra glow effects and keep it to just the eye glow for simplicity, then move to building the ground pad as a flat scaled cylinder with the ground color, possibly adding a subtler secondary ring for texture while staying within the limited color palette.

Now I'm thinking through grass tufts as small clusters of thin cone blades scattered near the fence base, but I need to watch the total part budget carefully since poles, bands, skulls, and pad elements are already adding up fast—I'll need to tally parts per component to keep things under the limit.

Let me reconsider the spacing: switching to 19 poles with a skull every third one gives 7 skulls symmetrically placed at both ends. Recalculating the totals with 38 for poles, 63 for skulls, and the rest unchanged lands around 162 elements, still under budget, so I'll trim the tufts down to 7 to stay safe.

Now I'm working out pole heights and proportions—regular poles varying between 0.7 and 1.2m with some sine-based variation, while skull poles get boosted to around 1.22-1.3m so their tops stay under the 1.5m ceiling once the skull geometry sits on top. I'm defining the shaft as a thin heptagonal cylinder with a cone tip, and for skull poles giving them a flat top with a short peg instead of the usual cone.

I'm also adding rope-band details that connect some of the poles together at mid-height, picking alternating pairs so the fence looks tied together rather than perfectly uniform.

Now I'm figuring out how the ropes sag between poles using a smooth curved sweep, attaching each end near the top of adjacent poles and letting the middle dip slightly. I'm keeping the pole bases flush with the ground pad so they look planted rather than floating.

Next I'm starting on little mushroom decorations with cream-colored stems and caps.

For the fence and mushroom placement, I'm working out coordinates so they stay clear of the leg positions near the center and sit sensibly relative to the pad radius and fence ring, tucking a few mushrooms near the back corners outside the main structure.

I'm placing grass tufts as small tilted cones along the inside of the fence base, and settling on the color palette—reusing the existing log, bone, and ground tones while adding two new greens for grass and keeping mushroom stems cream.

Now I'm writing a helper function to place parts with position, rotation, and scale, then building out the skull geometry using a local coordinate helper that maps right/up/forward offsets around a pole-top anchor point, starting with the cranium.

Still placing facial features...

Total parts land around 155. I'm placing skulls along pole angles from 70° to 290°, computing positions and yaw from the ellipse geometry, and varying heights for non-skull clutter with a capped max. That should fit within tolerance, so I'll write it out.

I'm setting up a buildLegs function that destructures the context object and reuses existing hip joints, planning the hip and knee chains for each leg.

Since hipL already exists as a joint, I realize I can't name a new chain hipL too — names must stay unique. Instead, I'll manually create kneeL and ankleL joints parented to the hip joint, then build sweeps across the bone path [hipL, kneeL, ankleL] so the thigh and shin are smoothly skinned.

Now I'm thinking through the anatomy more carefully — for a proper digitigrade chicken leg, the hip should sweep forward-down to the knee, then the tarsus angles down-back to the hock before the toes point forward again, so I'm sketching out approximate joint coordinates for hip, knee, and ankle to capture that silhouette.

Checking the hip-to-ankle distance confirms the two-segment leg reaches with a natural forward knee bend, so I'll build the leg as a limb chain from hip to knee to ankle, then add a separate foot joint from ankle to a ball point for the toe base.

I'm deciding to tie thigh and shin radii to hip/knee/ankle thickness, using one continuous sweep along the polyline with radii varying by parameter t, letting the skin round over the joint bends rather than sweeping each segment separately.

For shin bands, I'm considering alternating color rings instead, maybe using torus geometry oriented along the limb's tangent direction to create ring-like segments rather than splitting the tube mesh itself.

For bone assignment, since the path is built from literal points with no bone data, I should explicitly choose joints rather than rely on nearest-joint defaults — thigh rings bound to hipL, shin rings to kneeL, pulled from the chain's joints array. This keeps rings static and rigid near joints, which is fine since there's no bending animation happening here anyway.

Now I'm working out ring radius matching and sweep geometry, using octagonal rings slightly inflated to approximate the circumscribed torus radius. For the shin, I also want small flattened plates running down the front, which means figuring out the correct dorsal-facing clock angle along the sweep so the plates land on the right side of the limb.

I realize `chain.at(t)` is the better approach for the shin since it spans knee-to-ankle and carries proper bone attachment, unlike a bare frame which defaults to the nearest joint. So I'll loop through rows and use `b.ring(chain.at(t), {count:6, radius: r}, item => b.stick(plate, color, item))`, with `b.stick` orienting each plate outward along the frame's axis, scaling radius to match the shin's thickness at that point.

Now I'm budgeting parts: roughly 95 per leg, so with the sweep, knee ball, and 5 rings already accounted for, I'm considering limiting scale plates to the front-facing side only using ring's fromDeg/toDeg, since the shin tilts downward and slightly backward so I need to figure out which angle corresponds to "front."

Working out the feather tuft spikes around the thigh, computing radial offsets with a perpendicular basis to the thigh direction so the tufts point downward and outward, attached to the hip joint bone in layers.

Finishing feather counts, that gives 22 total combining both layers and knee fuzz.
